newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks skid as countdown to key vote begins.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks skid as countdown to key vote begins.

text.p: Indian shares skidded more than one percent on Friday as the government faced almost certain defeat in a key parliamentary confidence vote after talks to defuse a political crisis failed, analysts said.
"The market will move on political statements. Volumes are thin," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities, the Indian partner of Goldman Sachs & Co.
Analysts said lingering hopes that the federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March) would be passed despite the political turmoil capped the fall in stock prices.
"It looks like we are lurching towards elections," said Rupa Bose, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
"But the key issue for the market is whether the budget will be passed. It's almost become an independent issue," she said.
By noon (0630 GMT), Bombay's benchmark index was trading 45.41 points, or 1.26 percent, lower at 3552.96 -- and off its early low of 3512.05.
"We are asking investors to wait and watch for things to take shape," said Sanjeev Mohta, head of research at securities firm James Capel B&K. "The main issue remains the budget."

The fate of the market-friendly budget presented by Finance P. Chidambaram on February 28 was called into question on March 30 when the Congress party withdrew its make-or-break support for Prime Minister H. D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition.
Deve Gowda on Friday moved a vote of confidence in his government before the lower house of parliament.

Congress has ordered its 140 deputies to vote against the motion. Opposition rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its allies, with 193 votes, have also decided to vote against Deve Gowda.
But the BJP sought to allay fears in the business community by promising to help pass the budget after the vote.
"We are a responsible party," said BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj. "We can't trifle with the economic agenda of the nation."
Analysts said they were not worried by the growing prospects an early election -- the country's second this year.

"In our opinion an election might not be a bad idea to get the uncertainty out of the way, provided the winners get a clear mandate this time, even if it is the BJP," said Alok Sethi, director at Natwest Securities.
BJP officials have said the Hindu party was hoping for snap polls which surveys indicated would strengthen the BJP's hand in parliament.

"If the BJP comes to power I doubt if they would follow policies negative to industry and investment," Paribas Capital's Bose said. "It would not be in their interest to ferment any trouble or backtrack on economic reforms."
"The markets will see a bit of a roller coaster ride but if the index goes below 3000-3200 points, I would call a buy. I see no reason to panic," she added. --Bombay newsroom, (91) 22 265 9000
